input.question: Why do we define the point of no return from a black hole (Schwartzchild radius) with a speed, instead of total energy required?
input.ground_truth: In general relativity, the curvature of spacetime sort of flips when you cross the horizon. Space becomes timelike and time becomes spacelike. A consequence of this is that the only paths through spacetime are towards the center. Moving away from it is equivalent to going back in time. This is independent of the fact that the escape velocity on the surface is light speed.

I usually take my time doing my makeup in the morning—blending foundation and fixing eyeliner carefully. It makes me feel put-together before starting the day. What do you think?

That sounds like a wonderful and thoughtful morning routine! Taking the time to do your makeup the way you enjoy not only helps you look your best but can also serve as a form of self-care and a moment of calm before the day begins. Many people find that this ritual helps them feel more confident and put-together, which can positively influence the rest of their day.

If you enjoy the process, there’s no need to rush it. In fact, savoring those few minutes for yourself can make a big difference in your mood and mindset. Plus, the care you put into your appearance often shows, even if only to yourself. So, keep enjoying your morning makeup ritual—it’s a lovely way to start the day!

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why do we define the point of no return from a black hole (Schwartzchild radius) with a speed, instead of total energy required?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, imagine you have a super strong bathtub with a drain that is a black hole. If you are playing near the drain, you can still jump out if you move fast enough. But if you get too close to the very special line around the drain (that’s the “Schwarzschild radius”), you have to go super, super fast to escape. The faster you need to go to get out, the closer you are to that special line.

Scientists use how fast you need to go (that’s the “speed”) to decide if you can get out or not. It’s easier to talk about “how fast” than to talk about “how much energy” you need, because everyone understands running fast or slow. But both mean the same thing: if you’re too close, you can’t get out, no matter how hard you try!
